sources.title: Food production is responsible for one-quarter of the world’s greenhouse gas emissions (H. Ritchie, 2019)

facts.text: Food is responsible for about 26% of the world’s greenhouse gas emissions, roughly a quarter.
In 2018 Joseph Poore and Thomas Nemecek published, in the journal Science, the biggest review of food-system data up to then; it used data from over 38,000 commercial farms across 119 countries.
Food emissions are measured in kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalents, a unit that also counts other greenhouse gases such as methane and nitrous oxide according to how much warming they cause.
On average, producing 1 kilogram of beef from a beef herd releases 99.48 kg of carbon dioxide equivalents, while 1 kilogram of peas releases 0.98 kg.
In general, foods from animals have larger footprints than foods from plants.
Land use change and activities on the farm are the main sources of emissions for most foods, especially the largest emitters. Combined, they make up over 80% of the total for most foods.
Farm-stage emissions include the use of fertilizers, the handling of manure, and the methane produced in the stomachs of cattle.
Land use change releases carbon dioxide when forests, grasslands and other carbon sinks are turned into cropland or pasture.
For most food products transport makes up less than 10% of total emissions; for beef from beef herds it is about 0.5%.
Across the global food system, transport accounts for only about 6% of food’s emissions.
One study found that Swedish greenhouse tomatoes needed 10 times the energy of tomatoes shipped in from southern Europe, where the crop was then in season.
Moving food by plane emits about 50 times as much greenhouse gas as moving it by boat for each tonne carried one kilometer, but only 0.16% of food miles are by air.
Foods sent by air are mostly ones that spoil quickly, such as asparagus, green beans and berries.
A diet’s footprint shrinks far more through eating less meat and dairy, or replacing beef and lamb with chicken, pork or plant foods, than through buying local.
Eating local is often recommended as a way to cut the carbon footprint of a diet, and moving food from place to place does cause some emissions.

Worked out from the two datasets: transport is about 34% of the total for bananas (0.30 of 0.86 kg), about 10% for peas, about 6% for tofu, about 4% for poultry meat, about 2% for rice and for lamb, and under 1% for cheese and for beef.
